Project Zymera · working report

Teams of autonomous agents that hold together when one of their own works against them.

Zymera studies teams of autonomous agents — drones, vehicles, or software actors — that each act on local information and coordinate only through a short-range, shifting communication graph, pursuing a mission scored at the level of the team rather than the individual. Two questions run through the work.

Can the team generalize?

work in worlds it never trained on, transfer its skills, and reproduce its behavior reliably

Can it stay resilient?

survive a covert member that passes every local check yet quietly bends the mission — and we ask how far one can go

01Team & mission

What defines a team, and what defines a mission.

We keep these two definitions side by side, because the design that follows is an answer to their tension: a team this loosely coupled, chasing an objective it can only partly observe, has to work to stay coordinated at all.

The team

  • N autonomous agents — drones, vehicles, or software actors
  • decentralized — no controller sees or commands the whole
  • partial observation — each acts on its own local view
  • range-limited, time-varying comms — a graph G_t=(I,E_t)
  • redundant by design — several agents can cover for one

A mission

  • scored at the team level, not per agent
  • a coupling — how local work combines: Sense · Organize · Act
  • a contract — what's exchanged, and what's taken on trust
  • a health signal — a reading of capacity-to-continue, beyond reward

Three missions we instantiate, one frame each, drawn on the real generated worlds. The coupling is what each mission studies; the covert surface is where an insider would act.

CoverageSense · A
spread out and build a shared picture of an unknown world.
covert: report ground it never actually saw
Relay tetherOrganize · B
keep a moving lead linked back to base through a maze.
covert: report a healthy link as it quietly drops
CorneringOrganize · mixed
a pursuer team splits into squads, each cornering one evader (team vs team).
covert: a pursuer opens a small gap on the escape side

02From problem to design

The architecture follows from the problem.

Because the agents are many, decentralized, and each sees only part of the world, they have to share what they know; and because the channel between them is short-range and constantly shifting, a graph neural network operating over that communication graph is the natural way to do it. The rest of the choices fall out the same way — a centralized critic to assign credit while training but a decentralized actor to deploy, and connectivity handled as a soft constraint rather than a hard rule.

Why two message-passing rounds. Two rounds reach two hops, which is enough for an agent to take its neighbour and its neighbour's neighbour into account — the range at which local coordination actually happens. More rounds tend to oversmooth, pulling every agent's belief toward the same vector, and cost compute for reach the policy does not use. Max-aggregation is chosen for the same practical reason: it does not depend on how many neighbours there are, so a policy trained with four agents reads a ten-agent neighbourhood the same way.
Why connectivity stays soft. A hard rule that forbids any disconnecting move would make the graph unbreakable — and a team that cannot fracture has nothing to study about resilience. Keeping the constraint soft is what leaves the second question open at all.

03The system in one view

A decentralized actor, a centralized critic, one learning loop.

The actor is what runs on each agent. The critic exists only to compute advantages during training and is discarded at deployment. Everything below folds into a single PPO update.

belief b i,t
L3 · Decision — learned
from the fused belief, choose a goal and a role
goal / role
L2 · Planner — frozen
flood a value field to that goal (an exact wavefront)
value field
L1 · Controller & perception — scripted
climb the field one step, with a collision veto · SLAM · λ̂₂
move  a i,t
environment

Underneath the actor sits the training machinery: rollouts feed a PPO-clip objective and a GAE value loss, alongside a connectivity auxiliary λ̂₂ and an entropy term; a Lagrangian dual subtracts a connectivity penalty whose weight the training raises on its own; the critic pools all agents count-invariantly (setpool / setattn). The perception, belief, and comm graph feed back into the next decision — the loop shown on the right.

05The math that defines the setup

A few pieces worth stating precisely.

Less the standard machinery of reinforcement learning, and more the parts that are specific to a connected team moving through a walled world.

what it isthe expressionreads as
wall-RF occlusiona wall between two agents inflates the effective distance by the wall-runs k it crosses (with c=r/3), progressively weakening the link and dropping it only once d_eff passes range
local connectivity margina per-agent reading of "am I stretching the bridge?" — the shortfall in soft neighbours below a target
soft guardrail (no hard mask)connectivity as a learned constraint; the dual weight rises on its own until the team holds the graph
difference-reward creditan agent's credit is the ground only it added — the fix for the problem in §06
count-invariant critica mean over agents, so the same critic works at any team size
the connectivity barthe fraction of steps the whole team is connected — graded against a full one

06Heterogeneous credit assignment

When agents do different jobs, a shared reward misleads them.

Once a team differentiates, the reward has to differentiate with it. A relay that holds a link covers no new ground, while an explorer races across the map. Under a single shared return the relay's contribution is drowned out by the explorers', and the gradient it feels tells it to abandon its post and go explore — which is exactly what breaks the mission. This is the heterogeneous credit-assignment problem, and the usual MARL remedies (a shared return, or counterfactual baselines) are too coarse to separate the two roles.

How we handle it. An exact submodular difference reward gives each agent credit for precisely the cells only it provided, so a relay that added no coverage but kept the graph alive is rewarded through the connectivity term rather than punished by the coverage one. The same signal serves both measurement and training, and the per-agent credit doubles as a contribution estimate — the natural place for the covert-adversary detector to attach later.

07Emergence of collaboration

Division of labor appears, when the reward allows it.

We do not script roles. Under the right coupling, a team left with a shared coverage-and-connectivity reward will settle into a relay chain on its own — some agents holding the bridge while others push the frontier. But this is a conditional, weak kind of emergence: it shows up only while the connectivity constraint is soft. Harden it, or flatten the reward, and the team collapses back into a single homogeneous cluster.

Two caveats we keep in view. Coverage is submodular, so the team is never more than the sum of its parts — "emergence" here means a differentiation of behavior, not superadditivity. And adding agents tends to crowd rather than divide: our diagnostics show redundancy rising as the team grows, so turning that flooding into genuine division of labor remains the interesting open problem.

08Zero-shot to unseen worlds

Train on small worlds, deploy where you have never been.

A real deployment is never the training map, so generalization is treated as a first-class goal rather than a bonus. We train on small worlds and grade on unseen sizes and terrains with no fine-tuning; the different map styles — open, rooms, clutter, mixed, and structured mazes — exist precisely to catch a policy that only memorized.

what transfersresult
the size-invariant belief, trained at 16²/4 → deployed at 32²/1077–81% coverage with no fine-tuning  ·  a snapshot estimator manages 46%
an explicit planner in place of a reactive move head, on unseen maps79% reach  ·  25% for the reactive head — the gap is planning, not learning
coverage as a fraction of a god-view optimum, by terrainopen 72 · rooms 37 · mixed 31 · crowded 40

09How it moves, and how well it stays connected

Four terrains at 32×32, ten agents.

The same policy across four world types — each: 32×32, 10 agents, comm range 5, the distilled MVProp planner, seed 2, standard comm model (no wall-RF). Coverage varies with how much open ground there is; connectivity is full on open and simple rooms, and only slips on the most cluttered terrain.

Each panel plays on its own; use ❚❚ to pause and the slider to step through the episode by hand.

1/1
opencov 74% · conn 1.00
1/1
roomscov 30% · conn 1.00
1/1
mixedcov 30% · conn 0.94
1/1
cluttercov 57% · conn 0.85

On open and simple room layouts the team stays connected for the whole episode — λ₂ above the threshold at every step, a connectivity of 1.00 — while still covering three-quarters of the open world. Connectivity only softens on heavy clutter, where it settles around 0.85. Closing that last gap is a matter of the relay structure and some tuning rather than a missing capability, and the levers are in hand:

leverwhat it givesstate
relay roles (explorer / relay split)a structural backbone that holds the graphreaches 1.00 connectivity — at a coverage cost
connectivity-floor barriera firm push just before a link would snapbuilt, not yet tested in the matrix
a higher degree floor (≥ 2 neighbours)redundant links rather than a fragile chaina lever we have not swept
dual-rate tuninglet the constraint weight bind faster on clutterthe weight climbs but plateaus early

On the planner itself, a 72-run study (four variants across three terrains, three seeds, two scales) found the good planners interchangeable on the coverage-connectivity frontier, with one spatial-transformer variant clumping — buying connectivity by under-exploring. The planner is a navigation lever; connectivity is set by the reward, not by it.

10Reading the mission by its resilience

A team can earn reward while its capacity to continue erodes.

Because of that, resilience is read from the trajectory rather than the return: whether the team is in a viable state, whether it degrades along a slope or falls off a cliff, and whether it recovers. The load-bearing quantity is the break budget — the smallest number of compromised insiders that pushes the mission over the edge. For a relay it is a graph min-cut: a single chain fails at one, a redundant tether at its degree of redundancy. Redundancy is the defense, and the shape of the network is the break budget.

11Where things stand

In hand

  • size-invariant coverage that transfers 16² → 32²
  • a deterministic / distilled planner (79 vs 25 zero-shot)
  • full connectivity on open and room worlds
  • wall-RF occlusion in the comm model
  • relay division of labor under soft constraints
  • the resilience formalism — health, break budget, viability

Underway

  • the relay-tether mission, where decentralization is forced
  • the covert-insider threat model and a local detector
  • the goal-vs-move amplification experiment
  • multi-seed reporting for reproducibility

Still open

  • full connectivity on heavy clutter
  • turning flooding into true division of labor at scale
  • the coverage ceiling on the hardest terrains

12Where it is heading

The adversary comes back to a mature team.

The near path is the second question on the team we now have: introduce a stealth-bounded covert insider and measure how much more it costs when it corrupts a high-level goal than a low-level move — a single goal commits many steps, so the leverage is not the same. That comparison sits in a gap between the hierarchical-RL and the covert-MARL literatures.

Two further threads we hold lightly, as directions rather than commitments:

threadthe shape of the idea
Language models exploratorya slow-clock model that writes a reusable artifact — a reward, a role specification — which the fast controller then runs, kept out of the control loop and off the agent.
Energy-based methods exploratorya possible common lens for coverage and connectivity, read as a landscape the team descends — something to probe before committing to.
